title: Kabir the weaver
hookLine: Kabir of Benares, a weaver, sang in plain speech that no priest or custom stood between the soul and God

cards: Benares, on the Ganges: temples, priests, pilgrims, scholars arguing in Sanskrit. And in a narrow lane, the clack of a handloom. A weaver sits at it, throwing the shuttle back and forth, singing as he works.
Not in Sanskrit. In the plain speech of the street, sharp enough to make a priest wince and a laborer laugh. His name was Kabir, and the Sikh Gurus kept his songs in their book.

teach.b: Honest start: very little about Kabir's life is certain, and scholars disagree about his dates.
In his own verses he calls himself a julaha, a weaver; tradition says he grew up in a Muslim weaving family in Benares and learned from the Hindu teacher Ramanand.
Beyond that, much of what's told is legend. His songs are what remain, and the Guru Granth Sahib keeps a great many of them. What did he sing?
That nothing stands between the soul and God: not the priest, not the mullah, not birth, not pilgrimage.
In a hymn in Rag Gauri he turns on caste pride with a joke: if you're a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother, why didn't you come into the world by some other way? Everyone arrives the same way.
He was just as blunt about empty ritual in any religion. And the loom? In a hymn in Rag Gujri, his mother weeps: how will these children live?
Kabir has given up spinning and weaving and written God's Name on his body. Kabir answers that while threading the shuttle he forgets his Beloved, and that one Provider looks after them all.
So he made no neat peace with his trade. But he never stopped thinking like a weaver.

teach.h: GOD THE WEAVER, EARTH AND SKY THE LOOM.
teach.b: In Rag Asa he calls God the weaver whose secret no one knows, who stretched the warp of the whole world, earth and sky for a loom, sun and moon for two shuttles. A weaver's own tools became his picture of God at work.
Hence today's line: the loom is the prayer.

how: Kabir's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in Sikh kirtan alongside the Gurus' own, in the same ragas.

o: a priest who chants in Sanskrit
a weaver, someone who works at a loom
a wandering singer who begs for alms

games.q: who was Kabir — tap the pairs.
p: weeps that he left the loom

s: we know Kabir's life in great detail
we know very little for certain; his songs are what we have.
in one of Kabir's hymns, his mother worries that he has given up weaving
she weeps: how will these children live? he has written God's Name on his body instead.
Kabir sang in Sanskrit for scholars
he sang in the plain speech of the street.

games.q: a proud Brahmin tells Kabir that birth makes him holier. what does Kabir's hymn answer?
o: he jokes: if you're so different, why didn't you come into the world some other way?
games.why: in Rag Gauri, Kabir points out that everyone is born the same way; caste pride has nothing to stand on.

practice: Choose one task in front of you today: a job, a class, the dishes, a child's bedtime. Picture doing it the way Kabir sat at the loom, attentive, steady, every motion counted, not rushing to be done.
If you pray, let the rhythm of the work carry a word you remember by; if not, let it carry the breath.

wordCard.voice: Julaha, weaver. Kabir, a weaver of Benares whose plain, sharp songs, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, say nothing stands between the soul and God.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Kabir; an Arabic word, al-Kabir, 'the Great', one of the names of God in Islam.

carryVoice: Your line: the loom is the prayer. Even a shuttle can point to God. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 324 (Gauri Kabir: 'if you are a Brahmin, born of a Brahmin mother')
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 524 (Gujri Kabir: Kabir's mother weeps over the loom; Kabir answers)
Guru Granth Sahib, Asa Kabir, around Ang 484 (koree ko kaahoo maram na jaanaa: God the weaver, earth and sky the loom, sun and moon the shuttles)
